lessons.title: Identifying Engine Parts: Pistons, Rings, and Bearings
lessons.body: Pistons, rings, and bearings are the heart of any engine. In this lesson, you will learn to identify them by sight and touch. A piston is a cylindrical metal slug that moves up and down inside the cylinder. It has three or four grooves near the top. The top two grooves hold compression rings, which seal the combustion gases. The bottom groove holds the oil control ring, which scrapes excess oil off the cylinder wall. Rings are made of cast iron or steel and are split so they can spring into the groove. Bearings are smooth, curved metal shells that fit between moving parts to reduce friction. You will find main bearings (supporting the crankshaft) and connecting rod bearings (connecting the rod to the crankshaft). In African workshops, you often see pistons from Toyota, Nissan, and Mitsubishi engines. A 4-cylinder Toyota 3Y engine uses pistons with a 91 mm bore. Rings come in standard sizes (e.g., 0.25 mm, 0.50 mm oversize) for worn cylinders. To identify wear, check the ring end gap: insert a ring into the cylinder bore and measure the gap with a feeler gauge. If the gap exceeds 0.8 mm for a petrol engine, the rings are worn. Bearings show wear as scratches, pitting, or copper showing through the white metal layer. Always replace bearings in pairs (upper and lower). Use a micrometer to measure the crankshaft journal diameter; if it is more than 0.05 mm out of round, the crank needs grinding. In the field, you can use a plastigauge to check bearing clearance: place a strip on the journal, torque the cap, remove it, and compare the flattened width to the scale. Typical clearance for main bearings is 0.025Ã¢Â€Â“0.050 mm. Remember: clean hands and clean parts are criticalÃ¢Â€Â”dust in an engine kills it fast.

lessons.title: Removing and Replacing a Cylinder Head Gasket
lessons.body: A blown head gasket is one of the most common engine failures in Africa, often caused by overheating. Symptoms include white smoke from the exhaust, milky oil, and loss of coolant. To replace it, you need a torque wrench, socket set, scraper, and a new gasket. Start by disconnecting the battery negative terminal. Drain the coolant into a clean containerÃ¢Â€Â”you can reuse it if it's not contaminated. Remove the air cleaner, spark plug wires (label them), and any brackets attached to the head. Loosen the head bolts in the reverse of the tightening sequence (usually from outside to inside in a spiral). Never remove bolts when the engine is hotÃ¢Â€Â”let it cool completely to avoid warping. Lift the head straight up; it may be stuck, so tap gently with a rubber mallet. Clean the block and head surfaces with a scraper and brake cleaner. Check for warping with a straight edge and feeler gauge: if you can slide a 0.05 mm feeler under the straight edge, the head needs resurfacing. Clean the bolt holesÃ¢Â€Â”oil or dirt there gives false torque readings. Install the new gasket dry (unless it says otherwise) with the marking facing up. Oil the bolt threads lightly. Tighten in three stages: first to 30 Nm, then 60 Nm, then to the final spec (e.g., 80 Nm for a Toyota 3Y). Use a torque wrenchÃ¢Â€Â”never guess. After reassembly, refill with coolant, run the engine to operating temperature, and re-torque the head bolts after it cools. Retorque is critical; many gaskets fail again because this step is skipped. Finally, change the oil and filter to remove any coolant that leaked into the sump.

lessons.title: Checking and Replacing Spark Plugs in Petrol Engines
lessons.body: Spark plugs ignite the fuel-air mixture, and worn plugs cause rough idling, poor fuel economy, and hard starting. In Africa, you'll see plugs from NGK, Bosch, and Champion. To check them, first gather a spark plug socket (usually 16 mm or 21 mm), a ratchet, and a gap gauge. Work on a cold engine. Remove the plug wires one at a time, twisting the boot to break the seal. Use compressed air or a brush to clean around the plug before removingÃ¢Â€Â”otherwise dirt falls into the cylinder. Unscrew the plug and inspect it. A light tan or grey deposit means good running. Black soot means rich mixture or weak ignition. Oil fouling means worn rings or valve guides. White, blistered deposits mean overheating. Check the gap with a wire gauge: for most African petrol engines, the gap is 0.8Ã¢Â€Â“1.1 mm. If the gap is too large, tap the ground electrode gently; if too small, pry it open with the gauge. Replace plugs every 20,000Ã¢Â€Â“30,000 km for copper plugs, or 60,000 km for iridium. When installing, screw the plug in by hand first to avoid cross-threading. Then tighten with a torque wrench: 20Ã¢Â€Â“30 Nm for a 14 mm thread, 30Ã¢Â€Â“40 Nm for 18 mm. If you don't have a torque wrench, tighten until snug then another quarter turn. Apply a small amount of dielectric grease to the boot before reconnecting. Start the engine and listen for smooth running. If misfiring continues, swap the plug with another cylinder to see if the fault moves. Always replace all plugs at once for even performance.

lessons.title: Adjusting Valve Clearances on Common African Vehicles
lessons.body: Valve clearance is the small gap between the rocker arm and the valve stem. If too tight, valves don't close fully, causing compression loss and burnt valves. If too loose, you hear a tapping noise and valves don't open enough. Most African vehicles like Toyota Corolla, Nissan Sunny, and Mitsubishi Lancer have adjustable rockers. You need a feeler gauge set, a 10 mm and 12 mm spanner, and a screwdriver. Work on a cold engine (for most Japanese engines). Remove the valve cover. Rotate the crankshaft until the first cylinder is at top dead centre (TDC) on the compression stroke. You can tell by aligning the timing mark on the pulley with the pointer, and both rocker arms on cylinder 1 should be loose. Check clearance with the feeler gauge between the rocker and valve stem. For intake valves, typical clearance is 0.20 mm; for exhaust, 0.25 mm (check your manualÃ¢Â€Â”Toyota 3Y: intake 0.20 mm, exhaust 0.25 mm). If the gauge drags slightly, it's correct. To adjust, loosen the locknut, turn the adjusting screw until the feeler gauge slides with slight resistance, then hold the screw and tighten the locknut. Recheck after tightening. Then rotate the crank 180 degrees to bring cylinder 3 to TDC, adjust, then cylinder 4, then cylinder 2. For a 4-cylinder engine, firing order is usually 1-3-4-2. After all adjustments, reinstall the valve cover with a new gasket if hardened. Run the engine and listen for uniform tickingÃ¢Â€Â”no loud tapping. If you have a hydraulic lifter engine, no adjustment is needed; just keep oil clean. In dusty African conditions, check clearances every 20,000 km.

lessons.title: Diagnosing Common Engine Noises and Smoke
lessons.body: Engine noises and smoke tell you what's wrong. A deep knocking from the bottom end, especially when accelerating, usually means worn main or connecting rod bearings. A lighter, higher-pitched rattle from the top is often valve clearance too loose or worn camshaft lobes. A sharp pinging or knocking under load is pre-ignition, caused by wrong timing or low-octane fuel. A hissing sound near the exhaust manifold indicates a blown gasket. To diagnose smoke: blue smoke means burning oilÃ¢Â€Â”worn rings, valve guides, or turbo seals. White smoke (steam) means coolant entering the combustion chamber, often a blown head gasket or cracked head. Black smoke means too much fuelÃ¢Â€Â”dirty air filter, faulty injectors, or clogged return line. In Africa, black smoke is common in diesel engines with worn injectors. Use your senses: smell the smoke. Sweet smell = coolant; acrid = oil; sharp = fuel. Check oil level and condition: milky oil confirms coolant mixing. Do a compression test: remove all spark plugs, screw in the tester, crank the engine 4Ã¢Â€Â“6 times. Healthy petrol engine: 10Ã¢Â€Â“12 bar (145Ã¢Â€Â“175 psi). If one cylinder is low, pour a teaspoon of oil into it and retest. If pressure rises, rings are worn; if not, valves are bad. For noises, use a long screwdriver as a stethoscope: touch the tip to different parts and listen at the handle. Compare to a known good engine. Don't ignore noisesÃ¢Â€Â”they get expensive. A $5 bearing now saves a $500 crankshaft later.

lessons.title: Sourcing Reconditioned Engine Parts vs. New
lessons.body: In Africa, the choice between reconditioned and new parts is about cost, availability, and reliability. New parts are best for critical components like pistons, rings, and bearings if you can afford them. But many genuine new parts are expensive or counterfeit. Reconditioned partsÃ¢Â€Â”like a reconditioned cylinder head or crankshaftÃ¢Â€Â”are original parts that have been machined back to spec. They cost 40Ã¢Â€Â“60% less than new. However, quality varies. Buy from a reputable rebuilder who provides a warranty. Check for signs of good work: smooth surfaces, correct dimensions (use a micrometer), and no cracks (use dye penetrant or magnetic particle inspection). For African conditions, reconditioned alternators, starter motors, and brake calipers are often fine. But for internal engine parts, avoid cheap reconditioned pistonsÃ¢Â€Â”they may have worn ring grooves. Ask for the rebuilder's specs: piston-to-bore clearance should be 0.02Ã¢Â€Â“0.05 mm. For bearings, new is safer because reconditioned bearings are rare. When buying used parts from a scrapyard (common in Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa), inspect carefully. A used cylinder head must be pressure-tested for cracks. A used crankshaft must be measured for journal wear. Always compare prices from at least three suppliers. In many African cities, you can find importers of Japanese used engines (known as "half cuts") that include everythingÃ¢Â€Â”engine, transmission, and accessories. These are often a better deal than rebuilding your old engine. But check compression and oil pressure before buying. Finally, consider your use: for a taxi doing 200 km a day, buy new or high-quality reconditioned. For a farm truck, a good used part may suffice.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Engine Rebuild Tolerances, Torque Values, and Parts Sourcing for African Workshops

This practical reference lesson supports mechanics, workshop owners, and apprentices working on petrol and diesel engines common across Africa â Toyota 3Y/4Y, Nissan Z20/Z24, Mitsubishi 4G15/4G63, Isuzu 4JB1, and Peugeot 504/505 engines that still dominate the roads from Nairobi to Lagos to Accra. The goal is business-first: reduce comebacks, cut warranty losses, and increase profit per job by working to specification instead of by feel.

Every engine rebuild is a commercial decision. A workshop that measures clearances, torques to spec, and sources parts intelligently will charge the same labour rate as a workshop that guesses â but will keep the customer, avoid a free redo, and build a reputation that supports higher prices. This module gives you the numbers, the tolerances, and the sourcing logic to do that.

Why Tolerances Are a Business Issue

In many African workshops, an engine is judged "rebuilt" once new rings, bearings, and a gasket set are fitted. But if the bore is oval, the ring end gap is wrong, or the head bolts are torqued by feel, the engine will burn oil, smoke, and lose compression within a few thousand kilometres. The customer returns angry, the workshop loses the labour and the parts margin, and word spreads.

The numbers below are drawn from manufacturer service specifications for engines widely serviced in Africa. Always confirm against the specific engine's service manual â but these values give you a working reference for the most common families.

Table 1: Typical Rebuild Tolerances and Wear Limits â Common African Engines

Engine (common application) Bore Ã standard (mm) Max bore wear/taper (mm) Piston-to-bore clearance (mm) Top ring end gap (mm) Main bearing clearance (mm)
Toyota 3Y / 4Y (Hilux, Hiace, forklifts) 91.0 0.10 0.03â0.05 0.20â0.35 0.025â0.055
Nissan Z20 / Z24 (Datsun pickup, Urvan) 89.0 / 89.0 0.10 0.03â0.06 0.20â0.40 0.030â0.060
Mitsubishi 4G15 (Lancer, Colt) 75.5 0.08 0.02â0.04 0.20â0.35 0.020â0.050
Mitsubishi 4G63 (Pajero, L200) 85.0 0.10 0.03â0.05 0.25â0.40 0.025â0.055
Isuzu 4JB1 diesel (NKR, pickup) 93.0 0.12 0.05â0.08 0.30â0.50 0.040â0.080
Peugeot 504/505 XN1 (sedan, pickup) 88.0 0.10 0.03â0.06 0.25â0.45 0.030â0.060

Sources: Manufacturer service specifications compiled from Toyota, Nissan, Mitsubishi, Isuzu, and Peugeot workshop manuals; cross-checked against FAO Farm Machinery and Equipment Maintenance guidance and university extension engine overhaul notes. Values are indicative â always verify against the specific engine's service manual.

Table 2: Indicative Parts Pricing and Sourcing Comparison (East & West Africa, 2024)

Prices vary by country, import duty, and exchange rate. The table below shows typical relative costs based on workshop surveys in Kenya, Nigeria, and Ghana. Use it to decide when to recondition versus replace.

Component (engine family) New OEM (USD, indicative) New aftermarket (USD) Reconditioned / used (USD) Recommended route
Cylinder head gasket â Toyota 4Y 35â55 12â20 Not recommended New aftermarket or OEM
Piston + ring set â Nissan Z24 (per cylinder) 60â90 25â40 15â25 (used) New aftermarket for daily drivers
Main bearing set â Mitsubishi 4G63 70â110 30â50 Not recommended New only â bearings are wear items
Cylinder head (complete) â Isuzu 4JB1 450â700 250â400 120â200 (recon) Recon if pressure-tested and skimmed
Turbocharger â common diesel pickups 500â900 200â350 120â250 (recon) Recon from reputable rebuilder
Timing chain kit â Toyota 3Y 80â130 35â60 Not recommended New only

Sources: Indicative workshop pricing surveys, Nairobi (Kenya), Lagos (Nigeria), and Accra (Ghana), 2024; cross-referenced with regional auto parts distributor catalogues. Prices are for planning only and exclude labour, machining, and import duty.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Chemicals, Solvents, and Engine Fluids

Engine work exposes you to hazardous substances. Used engine oil contains carcinogenic polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and heavy metals; prolonged skin contact is linked to skin cancer. Carburettor and brake cleaners contain toluene, acetone, and methanol â use only in ventilated areas, away from sparks, and wear nitrile gloves and eye protection. Never use petrol (gasoline) as a washing solvent: it is highly flammable and its vapour can ignite from a hot manifold or static spark. Antifreeze (ethylene glycol) is toxic if swallowed and can cause kidney failure â store in labelled containers away from food and children. Brake fluid damages paint and is harmful if ingested. Asbestos may still be present in older clutch and brake linings from imported vehicles â never dry-brush or blow out dust; use wet methods and approved respiratory protection. Wash hands with soap and water, not solvent, before eating, drinking, or smoking. Dispose of used oil, filters, and solvents through licensed collectors â never into drains, soil, or open ground. For occupational chemical safety guidance, consult WHO and national occupational health authorities.

Quick Reference Checklist: Engine Rebuild Job Control

  1. Confirm the engine code and service manual before ordering any parts. A 4G63 for a Pajero may differ from a 4G63 in an L200. Wrong parts = lost margin and lost time.
  2. Measure before you buy. Use a bore gauge and micrometer to check bore wear, taper, and ovality. If wear exceeds the limit in Table 1, boring and oversize pistons are required â quote the customer before proceeding.
  3. Check ring end gap in the bore, not on the bench. File-fit only if the gap is below minimum; never file below the minimum specification.
  4. Torque in sequence, in stages. Cylinder head bolts: typically 3 stages (e.g. 30 Nm â 60 Nm â 90Â° angle) following the manual's pattern. Never reuse torque-to-yield (TTY) bolts.
  5. Verify bearing clearances with Plastigauge before final assembly. Record every reading on the job card â this protects you if the customer disputes the work.
  6. Pressure-test the cylinder head and check for cracks between valve seats before refitting. A cracked head found after assembly is a full redo at your cost.
  7. Price the job with a parts margin of 25â40% and a labour estimate that includes machining time. Never quote "from" prices â quote a range with a written diagnosis.
  8. Document the source of every part (OEM, aftermarket brand, reconditioned) on the invoice. This limits your liability and helps the customer understand the price difference.

Sourcing Logic: New, Aftermarket, or Reconditioned?

The decision is commercial, not emotional. For fleet and daily-driver customers, reliability matters more than the lowest price â recommend new aftermarket from a known brand (e.g. NPR, Taiho, Ajusa, Febi) or OEM. For a customer selling the vehicle soon, or a low-mileage second car, a properly reconditioned head or turbo from a rebuilder with a warranty can be the right call â provided you pass on the warranty terms in writing.

Never fit used bearings, used gaskets, or used timing components. These are wear items with no reliable remaining life. Reconditioned heads, cranks, and turbos are acceptable only when accompanied by a pressure test, crack test, and dimensional report. Build relationships with two or three reliable suppliers rather than chasing the cheapest price on every job â consistency protects your reputation.

For workshops in landlocked markets, freight and customs add 20â40% to landed cost. Ordering in bulk for common engine families (3Y, 4Y, Z24, 4G15) reduces per-unit cost and shortens vehicle downtime. Keep a small stock of high-turn items: head gaskets, ring sets, bearing sets, and timing kits for the top three engine families you service.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Farm Machinery and Equipment Maintenance (Agricultural Services Bulletin)
  • FAO â Guidelines for Agricultural Mechanization Policy and Workshop Practice
  • WHO â Guidelines on Occupational Health and Chemical Safety in Small Enterprises
  • ILRI â Publications on Machinery, Transport, and Rural Enterprise Development
  • MSD Manuals â Professional: Injuries and Poisoning (chemical exposure reference)

This lesson is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills programme, Course: Auto Parts & Assembly, Module 3. Always work to the specific engine manufacturer's service manual and local occupational safety regulations.

quiz.q: What is the function of the oil control ring on a piston?
options: B) Scrape excess oil off the cylinder wall
C) Transfer heat to the cylinder
D) Hold the piston pin in place
quiz.explanation: The oil control ring scrapes excess oil from the cylinder wall to prevent it from burning in the combustion chamber.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to measure the ring end gap?
quiz.explanation: A feeler gauge is inserted into the ring gap to measure its width.

quiz.q: What does a copper-colored streak on a bearing shell indicate?
options: C) Worn through the white metal layer
quiz.explanation: When the white metal layer wears away, the copper underlayer becomes visible, indicating the bearing needs replacement.

quiz.q: What is the typical main bearing clearance for a petrol engine?
quiz.explanation: Main bearing clearance is usually between 0.025 and 0.050 mm for most petrol engines.

quiz.q: Which symptom indicates a blown head gasket?
quiz.explanation: Milky oil is caused by coolant mixing with engine oil, a common sign of a blown head gasket.

quiz.q: When removing cylinder head bolts, in what order should you loosen them?
options: A) From center outward in a spiral
B) From outside inward in reverse of tightening sequence
C) Any order, it doesn't matter
quiz.explanation: Loosening in reverse of the tightening sequence prevents warping of the cylinder head.

quiz.q: What should you use to check if a cylinder head is warped?
options: B) Straight edge and feeler gauge
quiz.explanation: A straight edge placed on the head with a feeler gauge underneath reveals any warping.

quiz.q: Why should you clean the head bolt holes before installing bolts?
options: B) To ensure correct torque readings
C) To make bolts easier to turn
D) To remove old gasket material
quiz.explanation: Oil or dirt in the holes can cause false torque readings, leading to improper clamping force.

quiz.q: What is the correct spark plug gap for most African petrol engines?
quiz.explanation: Most petrol engines require a spark plug gap between 0.8 and 1.1 mm.

quiz.q: What does a black, sooty spark plug indicate?
quiz.explanation: Black soot on a spark plug indicates a rich fuel mixture or weak ignition.

quiz.q: When installing a spark plug, what should you do first?
options: C) Screw it in by hand
quiz.explanation: Screwing the plug in by hand first prevents cross-threading.

quiz.q: What is the recommended torque for a 14 mm spark plug?
quiz.explanation: A 14 mm spark plug typically requires 20Ã¢Â€Â“30 Nm of torque.

quiz.q: What happens if valve clearance is too tight?
quiz.explanation: Too tight clearance prevents valves from closing completely, causing compression loss and burnt valves.

quiz.q: For a Toyota 3Y engine, what is the typical intake valve clearance?
quiz.explanation: The Toyota 3Y engine specifies an intake valve clearance of 0.20 mm.

quiz.q: When adjusting valve clearances on a 4-cylinder engine with firing order 1-3-4-2, after adjusting cylinder 1 at TDC, which cylinder do you adjust next?
quiz.explanation: Following the firing order, after cylinder 1, you rotate the crank 180Ã‚Â° to bring cylinder 3 to TDC.

quiz.q: What is used to hold the adjusting screw while tightening the locknut?
quiz.explanation: A screwdriver is used to hold the adjusting screw to prevent it from turning while tightening the locknut.

quiz.q: What does blue smoke from the exhaust indicate?
quiz.explanation: Blue smoke is a sign of oil burning in the combustion chamber, often due to worn rings or valve guides.

quiz.q: A deep knocking noise from the bottom of the engine under acceleration usually means:
options: A) Worn main or rod bearings
quiz.explanation: Deep knocking from the bottom end is typically caused by worn main or connecting rod bearings.

quiz.q: What does a sweet smell in the exhaust smoke indicate?
quiz.explanation: A sweet smell is characteristic of coolant (ethylene glycol) burning in the combustion chamber.

quiz.q: During a compression test, if pressure rises after adding oil to a low cylinder, what is the likely problem?
quiz.explanation: If oil temporarily seals the rings and raises compression, the rings are worn.

quiz.q: What is a common use for a long screwdriver when diagnosing engine noises?
quiz.explanation: Placing the tip on engine parts and listening at the handle helps locate the source of noises.

quiz.q: What is the typical compression pressure for a healthy petrol engine?
quiz.explanation: A healthy petrol engine typically produces 10Ã¢Â€Â“12 bar (145Ã¢Â€Â“175 psi) of compression.

quiz.q: Why is it important to check for cracks in a used cylinder head?
options: B) Cracks can lead to coolant loss and overheating
quiz.explanation: Cracks in the cylinder head can allow coolant to enter the combustion chamber or leak externally, causing overheating.

quiz.q: What is a 'half cut' in the African used car parts market?
options: A) A cut in half engine block
B) A front half of a Japanese used car including engine and transmission
quiz.explanation: A half cut is the front section of a used Japanese vehicle, often including the engine, transmission, and accessories.

quiz.q: When buying reconditioned pistons, what specification is critical?
quiz.explanation: Piston-to-bore clearance must be within specification (e.g., 0.02Ã¢Â€Â“0.05 mm) for proper fit and function.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a good reconditioned part?
options: A) Smooth surfaces and correct dimensions
quiz.explanation: A good reconditioned part will have smooth surfaces, correct dimensions, and no cracks or excessive wear.

quiz.q: What should you do before buying a used engine from a scrapyard?
options: B) Check compression and oil pressure
quiz.explanation: Checking compression and oil pressure helps assess the internal condition of a used engine.

quiz.q: For a taxi doing high mileage, what is the best choice for engine parts?
options: B) New or high-quality reconditioned parts
quiz.explanation: High-mileage vehicles require reliable parts to avoid frequent breakdowns; new or quality reconditioned parts are best.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a plastigauge?
quiz.explanation: Plastigauge is a thin plastic strip used to measure bearing clearance by crushing it between the journal and bearing.

quiz.q: When replacing a head gasket, why should you retorque the head bolts after running the engine?
options: B) To compensate for gasket compression
quiz.explanation: The gasket compresses after heating and cooling cycles, so retorquing ensures proper clamping force.
